intro: Stories are grouped by the four roles the system actually implements (users.role): Staff, Supervisor, HR Manager and Administrator. A story is listed under the role that initiates it.

Acceptance criteria are written against observed behaviour, so each one is checkable. The Implemented by line names the route or class that satisfies the story, which is what makes this a traceability artefact and not a wish list.
note: The role matrix these are derived from is HIMS_SYSTEM_DOCUMENTATION.md §3.1; per-screen visibility rules are in HIMS_ACCESS_AND_VISIBILITY.md.

roles.blurb: A clinical or administrative employee with a login. Sees their own record and the hospital-wide surfaces, and nothing about anyone else's performance.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to see my own competency gaps and credential expiries on one dashboard, so that I know what to fix before someone tells me.
ac: The dashboard shows my competency count, average gap and next credential expiry.
It shows no figures for any other employee.
A credential inside 30 days of expiry is banded expiring; past its date it is banded expired — computed on read, never from a stored column.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to read the review my supervisor wrote about me, so that the feedback reaches me rather than sitting in a file.
ac: I can open reviews where I am the subject.
I can see per-KPI ratings, comments, strengths and improvement notes.
I cannot open a review belonging to anybody else.
I cannot change any score.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to write a response to a finished review and later acknowledge it, so that my side is on the record without altering the reviewer's assessment.
ac: Response submission opens once the reviewer marks the review finished.
Acknowledgement becomes available only once the cycle is completed.
Submission and acknowledgement are timestamped separately.
Acknowledging locks my response permanently.
Reviewer scores remain unchanged and remain the source of record.
Both events land in audit_trails as review_employee_response / review_acknowledged.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to log my CPD hours and see which of them have been verified, so that I can tell a real total from a claimed one.
ac: I can log a CPD record from a modal on the CPD page.
Each record shows its verification state.
Only verified hours count toward a renewal cycle.
My own CPD page lists only my records.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want one page listing the training assigned to me and how far off I am, so that I am not surprised by a deadline.
ac: The page lists every assignment naming me, whether directly or by department, role or all-staff fan-out.
Each row shows its due date and my completion state.
A null required_by is never shown as overdue.
Overdue uses the same definition as every other screen.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to register for a training session and be checked in when I attend, so that attendance is a record of presence and not of intent.
ac: I can self-register for an upcoming session.
Registration is refused when the session is full.
Only a supervisor or above can mark me attended — check-in is the sole attendance mechanism for sessions.
I can submit feedback on a session I attended.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to recognise a colleague publicly or privately, so that appreciation is attributable either way.
ac: A post names both sender and recipient in either mode.
Self-recognition is refused.
A private post is visible only to sender, recipient and HR/Admin moderators.
Comments and reactions inherit the post's audience.
Only approved public posts appear on the wall and in the leaderboard.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want to ask the assistant a question in plain language, so that I do not have to know which module holds the answer.
ac: The assistant rail opens from the topbar on any page.
Answers are limited to data my role and reporting line already permit.
My saved conversations are visible only to me.
A provider outage returns a readable warning instead of an error page.

stories.story: As a staff member, I want search and notifications to only ever take me somewhere I am allowed to be, so that the shell never dangles a link that then refuses me.
ac: Search results come from an explicit source allow-list, each applying its module's scope before matching.
A row-level result scrolls to the row it names.
A notification about an employee I cannot see falls back to the module page rather than a forbidden deep link.
Read notifications stay visible; only their emphasis and the unread count change.

roles.blurb: A people manager. Reach is the reporting line — the employees whose supervisor_id is this account's linked employee_id — plus themselves. Not the department.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want my dashboard and team lists to show my direct reports, so that I am accountable for a defined set of people.
ac: Core figures, team list, hotspots and recent reviews are direct-report scoped.
An employee who merely shares my department does not appear.
Credential alerts remain department-scoped and upcoming sessions remain hospital-wide — this mix is deliberate.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to create a review only for someone I actually supervise, so that the dropdown itself states who I may legitimately assess.
ac: The employee list on the create screen contains only legitimate subjects.
reviewer_id === employee_id is refused — there is no self-review.
There is no peer review; a review carries one voice, supervisor_score.
Creating a review in a cycle that has already ended is refused.
A second review for the same person and cycle redirects to the existing one instead of inserting.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to score a review against the KPI grid and see each KPI's real share of the final number, so that the weighting I am told about is the weighting that was applied.
ac: Each KPI takes a 1–5 rating and an optional comment.
The screen distinguishes Average of KPI ratings from Final Score / weighted by KPI importance and says why they differ.
Per-KPI share is apportioned by largest remainder so the column totals exactly 100%.
An unrated KPI leaves the denominator entirely rather than counting as zero.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want a review to stop being editable when its cycle ends, so that the freeze does not depend on anyone remembering to close it.
ac: Editability is derived from review_cycles.end_date on every read.
A cycle ending today is open all day; the day after, writes are refused.
Only draft and finished are settable by hand; completed is nobody's to set.
The freeze holds with no scheduler running.
Any query for open reviews joins the cycle — the status column alone cannot answer it.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to assess competencies and record credentials for my reports, so that the gap register reflects what I have observed.
ac: Assessment and credential creation happen in modals on the competency page.
The employee list is scoped to my reports.
The gap is computed by the database, not typed in.
The change is written to audit_trails.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to record a course completion for a report, so that nobody self-certifies their own mandatory training.
ac: Completion requires the record-completion gate and a supervisor-or-above role.
I can only record it for my own direct reports.
Completion credits a verified CPD record worth the course's cpd_hours.
Reopening is admin/HR only, because it withdraws evidence and deletes the CPD row.
Sessions are never completed this way — check-in is their only mechanism.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to see an AI gap narrative grounded in what was actually written about my report, so that the advice cites evidence rather than inventing it.
ac: The prompt receives the verbatim strengths, improvements and per-KPI comments across the last three cycles.
The screen renders the same grouped feedback the prompt was built from.
A cycle with nothing written is stated as an absence, not dropped.
When comment sharing is switched off, the model is told the text was withheld.
Comments are truncated for the prompt only; the screen shows them in full.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to develop succession candidates from my own reports without seeing confidential ratings, so that development is possible without disclosure.
ac: I see only positions and candidates relevant to my direct reports.
Performance and potential scores, 9-box label, readiness, mentor and candidate status are redacted for me.
HR and Admin retain those fields.
I can still record leadership development milestones for my reports.

stories.story: As a supervisor, I want to assign required training to a person, a department, a role or everyone in one submission, so that a mandate does not take twenty clicks.
ac: One modal posts subjects[] mixing course:<uuid> and session:<uuid> values.
One training_assignments row is created per subject, inside one transaction.
Both subject lists are searchable checkbox lists; filtering never clears a ticked box.
Roster visibility is filtered to what I may see, even where the target expanded globally.

roles.blurb: Hospital-wide reach over the development modules and the confidential succession fields, but — deliberately — no blanket authority to review anybody.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want to open review cycles and maintain the KPI library, so that a review period has a defined start, end and measure.
ac: Cycles come in four types and are created and edited from modals.
A KPI carries target, unit, weight and applicable roles.
A weight is meaningful only next to the other weights on the same review.
Editing a cycle returns me to the page I opened the modal from.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want to review outside the reporting line only on a stated, logged basis, so that the exception is visible rather than assumed.
ac: My role grants no blanket review access.
Exactly four bases are valid: no_supervisor, supervisor_unavailable, supervisor_is_subject, supervisor_account_unavailable.
Each requires a typed reason.
The basis and reason are stamped on the review, badged in the UI, and written to audit_trails as review_exception.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want renewal rules and per-employee cycles, so that a licence requirement is enforced against the window it applies to.
ac: A rule opens a cycle per employee with the requirement frozen at hours_required_snapshot.
Attained hours are summed from verified CPD on every read, never stored on the cycle.
Risk is rated at risk / shortfall / met from the current window.
A caller may hand in a visibility scope so the at-risk list respects reporting lines.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want an accreditation report I can hand to a surveyor, so that evidence is produced rather than assembled by hand.
ac: One row per active employee.
Filterable by department, role and JCI standard.
The JCI code is read from competency_categories, one join above the competency.
Counts and badges are rendered together in the same cell.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want to know which employees are tracked without a login, so that a compliance gap is not mistaken for an account gap.
ac: The report names proxy-tracked employees and orphaned logins separately.
Compliance still governs an employee with no users row — the layer keys off employee_id only.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want a 9-box succession grid with the confidential fields intact, so that pipeline decisions can be made on complete information.
ac: Critical positions, candidates and readiness are visible hospital-wide.
The 9-box placement is derived in PHP from performance and potential.
Readiness evidence draws on competency and credential standing.
A quarterly review stamp can be recorded against a position.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want to moderate recognition and manage badges, so that the wall stays appropriate without becoming anonymous.
ac: Moderation requires the manage-recognition gate.
Moderators can see private posts for moderation purposes.
Every moderation act is audited.
Sender and recipient stay identifiable in both modes.

stories.story: As an HR manager, I want expiring credentials to reach the employee, their supervisor and their department head, so that a lapse is somebody's problem before it becomes everybody's.
ac: A daily command scans expiry windows.
The alert-log ledger is the single dedupe path, so a re-run does not re-notify.
Escalation reaches all three recipients.
A department head who is out of chain gets the module page, not a forbidden deep link.

roles.blurb: Full functional reach plus account and platform administration. Still not exempt from review-authority rules.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want to provision accounts myself, so that nobody self-registers into a hospital system.
ac: Public registration is disabled.
I set the role and optionally link a users.employee_id.
Passwords are hashed with bcrypt at cost 12.
Five failed attempts lock the account.
Account changes are audited.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want the org chart separated from account permissions, so that promoting someone to manager is not the same act as granting them privileges.
ac: employees.is_people_manager drives the org chart; users.role drives permissions.
A Reports To change cannot create a cycle in the reporting graph.
The change is audited.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want to control what employee text may leave the hospital for an AI provider, so that data sharing is a decision rather than a default.
ac: ai_include_comments = '0' stops written review comments reaching the provider entirely.
ai_redact_names blanks the subject's name parts and any Patient/Pt.-prefixed identifier.
Any read error on the settings table redacts rather than opens up.
The switches are read by the prompt builder itself, not by each caller.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want to change AI provider without changing consumer code, so that a vendor decision is configuration.
ac: Consumers depend on the AiProvider contract only.
AI_PROVIDER selects gemini, openai, anthropic or compatible; gemini is the default.
Model is env-configurable per provider.
A provider failure returns a warning string and never throws.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want the assistant to be able to perform writes on my behalf under the same RBAC as the UI, so that convenience does not become escalation.
ac: The registry holds 30 actions, each derived from the route's own middleware.
A role check runs before the entity resolver.
Names are resolved to UUIDs rather than guessed.
A destructive plan requires explicit confirmation.
Every executed write is audited as an AI action.
Registry keys point at .store routes, never .create — which is what made deleting the GET create pages safe.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want an audit endpoint over the recorded rows, so that sensitive changes are attributable — while knowing the coverage is partial.
ac: /audit/history is HR/Admin only.
Rows carry actor, action, table, record and timestamp.
Ordinary reads and many ordinary UI edits are not tracked.
There is no hash chaining, and the table is not to be read as a complete history.

stories.story: As an administrator, I want a release's markup to be served with that release's stylesheet, so that a new component cannot render bare behind a four-hour cache.
ac: Both unbuilt static assets append substr(md5_file($path), 0, 8).
The stylesheet is loaded only via @include('partials.app-css').
All four standalone <head> blocks go through the partial.
A bare asset('css/hims.css') anywhere fails the contract test.
